stem: A 32-year-old patient presents with small, well-demarcated, scaly plaques on the elbows and knees, involving less than 5% of the body surface area. The patient reports mild itching but is otherwise healthy. Considering the extent and severity of the disease, which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?
stemHtml: Q 04: A 32-year-old patient presents with small, well-demarcated, scaly plaques on the elbows and knees, involving less than 5% of the body surface area. The patient reports mild itching but is otherwise healthy. Considering the extent and severity of the disease, which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy? (Question Id: 515020)
keywords: “<5% body surface area” – Indicates limited/mild psoriasis, pointing to topical therapy.
“Small, well-demarcated, scaly plaques” – Classic description of plaque psoriasis, confirming the type of lesion.
“Mild itching, otherwise healthy” – Suggests mild disease with no systemic involvement, ruling out systemic therapy.
keywordsHtml:
1. “<5% body surface area” – Indicates limited/mild psoriasis, pointing to topical therapy.
  2. “Small, well-demarcated, scaly plaques” – Classic description of plaque psoriasis, confirming the type of lesion.
  3. “Mild itching, otherwise healthy” – Suggests mild disease with no systemic involvement, ruling out systemic therapy.

D.title: Topical corticosteroids
D.body:
Topical corticosteroids are first-line therapy for limited plaque psoriasis (<5% body surface area).
They reduce inflammation, erythema, and scaling by inhibiting keratinocyte proliferation, and suppressing local immune responses in the skin.
Potency is selected based on lesion location (low-medium potency for face/flexures, high potency for elbows/knees).
Safe for short-term and intermittent use, and effective in mild, localized disease.
D.bodyHtml:
• Topical corticosteroids are first-line therapy for limited plaque psoriasis (<5% body surface area).
  • They reduce inflammation, erythema, and scaling by inhibiting keratinocyte proliferation, and suppressing local immune responses in the skin.
  • Potency is selected based on lesion location (low-medium potency for face/flexures, high potency for elbows/knees).
  • Safe for short-term and intermittent use, and effective in mild, localized disease.

A.title: Systemic corticosteroids
A.body:
Not recommended for psoriasis due to risk of rebound flares and pustular psoriasis upon withdrawal.
Reserved only for severe, refractory cases or specific complications.
A.bodyHtml:
• Not recommended for psoriasis due to risk of rebound flares and pustular psoriasis upon withdrawal.
  • Reserved only for severe, refractory cases or specific complications.

B.title: PUVA (Psoralen + UVA therapy)
B.body:
Used in moderate to severe or extensive psoriasis, not for limited disease.
Requires multiple sessions and monitoring for skin cancer risk and phototoxicity.
B.bodyHtml:
• Used in moderate to severe or extensive psoriasis, not for limited disease.
  • Requires multiple sessions and monitoring for skin cancer risk and phototoxicity.

C.title: Biologics
C.body:
Reserved for moderate to severe plaque psoriasis or cases unresponsive to topical/systemic therapy.
High cost and potential immunosuppression; overkill for <5% BSA involvement.
C.bodyHtml:
• Reserved for moderate to severe plaque psoriasis or cases unresponsive to topical/systemic therapy.
  • High cost and potential immunosuppression; overkill for <5% BSA involvement.

E.title: Methotrexate
E.body:
Systemic therapy for severe, extensive, or rapidly progressing psoriasis.
Requires monitoring for hepatotoxicity and myelosuppression, so not suitable for mild, localized disease.
E.bodyHtml:
• Systemic therapy for severe, extensive, or rapidly progressing psoriasis.
  • Requires monitoring for hepatotoxicity and myelosuppression, so not suitable for mild, localized disease.

keyConcept:
Mild, limited plaque psoriasis (<5% BSA) is treated first-line with topical corticosteroids.
Systemic therapies (methotrexate, biologics, systemic corticosteroids, PUVA) are reserved for moderate to severe or refractory disease.
keyConceptHtml:
• Mild, limited plaque psoriasis (<5% BSA) is treated first-line with topical corticosteroids.
  • Systemic therapies (methotrexate, biologics, systemic corticosteroids, PUVA) are reserved for moderate to severe or refractory disease.

metadata.mcqTitle: Classification & Variants - Plaque Psoriasis – Mild / Limited Disease Management

table1.heading: Dermatology – Plaque Psoriasis – Mild / Limited Disease Management

cells: Definition / Extent
Plaque psoriasis involving <5% body surface area

Usually limited to:
elbows,
knees,
scalp
Clinical Features

Small, well-demarcated, scaly plaques;
mild itching

Common sites: extensor surfaces;
no systemic involvement
First-line Therapy
Topical corticosteroids

Low-to-medium potency for face/flexures;
high potency for elbows/knees
cellsHtml:
• Low-to-medium potency for face/flexures;
  • high potency for elbows/knees

cells: Other Topical Options

Vitamin D analogs (calcipotriol),
coal tar,
moisturizers
Can be combined with corticosteroids for synergistic effect
cellsHtml: • Can be combined with corticosteroids for synergistic effect

cells: Systemic / Advanced Therapy
Reserved for moderate to severe psoriasis

Methotrexate, biologics, PUVA;
not indicated for <5% BSA
Follow-up / Monitoring

Assess response in 2–4 weeks;
monitor for side effects
Educate patient on intermittent use and adherence
cellsHtml:
• Assess response in 2–4 weeks;
  • monitor for side effects
• Educate patient on intermittent use and adherence

table2.heading: Differential Diagnosis of Mild / Limited Plaque Psoriasis

cells: Eczema / Atopic Dermatitis

Pruritic,
erythematous,
sometimes oozing plaques

Typically ill-defined borders,
more flexural involvement,
acute flares
Tinea corporis (Fungal infection)

Annular,
scaly plaques with central clearing
cellsHtml:
• Positive KOH mount;
  • often single or few lesions;
  • responds to antifungals

cells: Lichen planus

Purple,
flat-topped,
polygonal papules
cellsHtml:
• Violaceous color, Wickham striae;
  • usually pruritic;
  • mucosal involvement possible

cells: Seborrheic dermatitis

Greasy,
yellowish scales on scalp,
face, chest

Distribution favors seborrheic areas;
less sharply demarcated
Pityriasis rosea
Herald patch followed by Christmas-tree pattern

diagram.heading: Plaque Psoriasis: Mild / Limited Disease Management
diagram.description: The diagram illustrates mild plaque psoriasis (<5% BSA) with small, well-demarcated scaly plaques on elbows and knees, highlighting first-line treatment with topical corticosteroids, vitamin D analogs, and moisturizers. It also shows follow-up recommendations and indicates advanced therapies (methotrexate, biologics, PUVA) reserved for moderate to severe or uncontrolled disease (>10% BSA).
